title: The daughter who argued
hookLine: Princess Ruja rescues her father from a false teaching (Jataka 544)

cards: On a bright festival night, King Angati of Mithila asks his advisers what would make the evening complete. One suggests visiting a well-known ascetic.
The ascetic, Guna, tells the king something that sounds like freedom: there is no fruit of deeds. Good or bad, nothing you do comes back. What will be, will be.
The king goes home convinced. Today, the person who argues him out of it: his daughter.

teach.b: Angati stops giving. He closes his gifts to the poor and turns to his own pleasures, since nothing, he now believes, makes a difference.
Then Princess Ruja comes to him, as she regularly does, to ask for money for her own gifts. He refuses and explains his new view. And she argues.
Respectfully, calling him father, but she doesn't back down. The story says she could remember past lives, and she tells him of one where a wrong she did came back to her in suffering.
Deeds have fruit, she says; she has seen it. The king won't move.
So Ruja turns to the directions and asks, in effect, for any good being in the world to come and help.
Narada, a being from a high heaven, comes down dressed as an ascetic, and with patience and vivid pictures of where deeds lead, brings the king back to giving and to his precepts.
Tradition pairs this tale with equanimity, upekkha. The one who stands up to the false teaching isn't a sage or a minister.

It's a daughter, speaking up at home, to her own father, with no guarantee he'll listen. She argues with love, not contempt, and she asks for help when her own words run out. That's the shape of disagreeing well.

how: Buddhist teaching holds that intentional actions, kamma, bear fruit; the tale of Ruja and Narada is told to show why that teaching matters for how a person lives and gives.

the princess who argued with her father
a queen who gave alms on festival days

games.q: who did what in Ruja's story: tap the pairs.
p: taught there's no fruit of deeds
came down and brought him back

s: Ruja won the argument on her own
the king wouldn't move; she asked for help, and Narada came.
Ruja drew on memories of her past lives
the story says she remembered past lives and told of a wrong that came back to her.
the false teaching said deeds have no fruit

games.q: you're Princess Ruja. your father refuses you, saying deeds have no fruit. what do you do?
o: argue respectfully from what you've seen.
games.why: she argues with respect, telling of a past life, and when he won't move, she asks for any good being to help.

practice: Choose a small belief you've taken as settled, like nothing changes anyway, or they'll never listen, and hold it up to the light: what have you actually seen?
Don't attack it or defend it; just ask, the way Ruja asked her father, with respect and without backing down.

wordCard.voice: Ruja. The king's daughter who argued against his belief that deeds have no fruit, and asked the heavens for help when her own words ran out.

orig.note: Pali kamma, deed or action; Sanskrit karma. Guna denied its fruit; Ruja defended it.

carryVoice: Your line: the daughter argued. Respect and disagreement can share one voice. That's day eight hundred forty-four.
